courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Projecting Gaussians to splats and sorting them by tile
md: The sort is per tile, by each Gaussian's center depth, not per pixel. Where two large splats interpenetrate, the true order can differ from pixel to pixel, so blending is approximate. The paper notes this error becomes negligible as splats shrink toward pixel size, and lists sudden order switches (popping) as a limitation.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers and epochs: stop reuse while anyone looks
md: "Garbage collection solves ABA" is a common misconception that Michael calls out. GC prevents ABA caused by *reuse*, but if a program moves the same nodes back and forth between two lock-free stacks, a node can leave and return to the same position with perfect GC. Ask whether the algorithm is ABA-safe under GC first; only then do hazard pointers or epochs make it ABA-safe without GC.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Reporting an ablation people can trust
md: Report per-stage deltas with intervals, the paired test and effect size, win/loss counts, interaction cells for stages that depend on each other, and cost, all on one stated harness. A bare column of mean scores invites the wrong conclusion.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Mass assignment and property-level authorization
md: Field lists rot in one direction: new fields. A blocklist that forbids `isAdmin` today silently allows `isOwner` added next quarter. An allowlist forgets a new field by leaving it read-only, which fails safe.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: NTLM: challenge and response, and why the hash is enough
md: NTLM never sends the password, but its proof is computed only from the unsalted NT hash plus a server challenge. So the hash is the password. Move to NTLMv2 only, then to Kerberos, and watch 4776 and the 4624 package name.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: DCSync: asking a domain controller for every password
md: 4662 is only written if Directory Service Access auditing is on **and** the domain object's SACL asks for it. Many domains have neither, and then DCSync leaves no Security log trace at all. Check before you need it.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Why documents and scripts: the chain an analyst unpicks
md: The first file is rarely the payload. Treat a maldoc, script or shortcut as a list of instructions: read every instruction, follow each stage on paper, and collect indicators at every hop, not only at the end.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Unpacking I: what a packed file looks like, using UPX
md: Section names prove nothing. Whoever builds a file chooses them, so UPX0 may hold a different packer's code and a custom packer may name its sections .text. Trust the measurable signals (entropy, sizes, permissions, imports, entry point) and confirm in a debugger.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Information leaks: why modern exploits start by reading
md: Treat any leak of a pointer, canary or uninitialized byte across a trust boundary as a security bug in its own right. In modern exploits the leak is often the second bug that makes the first one usable.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Deconfliction: is this the red team or a real intruder?
md: Deconfliction protects the organisation, not the red team. Every alert goes through normal escalation; the control group answers "ours or not" from precise operator logs; anything that does not match is a real incident; and the red team pauses when a real intruder may be present.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Regulated red teaming: TIBER-EU, DORA and CBEST
md: Regulated schemes formalise everything in this course: intelligence chooses the adversary, a small control team holds the secret and the stop button, flags define success, leg-ups are logged, every action is recorded, and the test ends in a replay and purple teaming rather than a pass mark.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: From one model call to an agent loop
md: A harness is a loop: call the model, run the tool calls it asks for, append the results, repeat until the model returns no tool calls or a budget runs out. Everything else (context management, permissions, traces, evals) is infrastructure around that loop.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: The write path: extract facts, dedupe and resolve conflicts
md: Misconception: conflict resolution is a database problem you can solve with "latest write wins". Whether two facts conflict is a judgment about meaning ("eats fish" vs "vegetarian" share no words), which is why Mem0 asks an LLM. That also means the resolver can be wrong: a sarcastic "oh sure, I love meetings" can delete a real preference.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Why intrinsic self-correction often fails
md: Self-correction works when the feedback carries information the generator did not have: a failing test, a compiler error, a schema violation, a human note. Asking the same model to "check again" adds calls, not information.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Direct and indirect injection, and how jailbreaks differ
md: Hidden does not mean exotic. White text, zero-size fonts, HTML comments, alt text, document metadata and invisible Unicode characters are all ordinary ways text reaches a model without a human noticing. If your extractor keeps it, the model reads it.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: RAG and vector stores: poisoning and permission leaks
md: Filtering after the model answers is too late: the model has already read the forbidden chunk and may paraphrase it. Filter before the chunk enters the context, using the same permissions as the source system, kept in sync when they change.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Stability: formation energy and energy above the convex hull
md: The hull test is a 0 K, zero-pressure, ordered-crystal calculation (the Materials Project docs state the 0 K, 0 atm assumption). It ignores entropy, so it can favor artificially ordered arrangements of similar atoms that would be disordered at real synthesis temperatures. "On the hull" means "thermodynamically plausible in DFT", not "can be made in a lab".

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Detection is a z-test on the green count
md: The normal approximation is optimistic for short texts. For $T = 50$, $\gamma = 0.25$ and 25 green tokens, $z = 4.08$ and the normal tail is $2.2 \times 10^{-5}$, but the exact binomial tail is $1.2 \times 10^{-4}$, about 5.5 times larger. Use the exact binomial when T is small.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: What an allocation trace records and why you would replay it
md: Live bytes are not RSS. RSS counts whole pages the process has touched, including allocator metadata, rounding and free holes. The gap between the two is the overhead you are usually hunting.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Local Outlier Factor: density compared with your neighbors
md: scikit-learn's LocalOutlierFactor has two modes. With novelty=False (the default) only fit_predict and negative_outlier_factor_ exist. With novelty=True you get predict, decision_function and score_samples, but the docs warn to call them only on new data: scoring the training points that way gives wrong results, and predict will not match fit_predict.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: API keys, bearer tokens and session cookies
md: An API key in a mobile app or a web page is public. Anyone can unpack the app and read it. Keys that must stay secret belong on servers; a client that runs on the user's device needs a per-user token instead. Defender view: a fixed prefix like `sk_` lets secret scanners find leaked keys in code; log the key id (never the secret) per request and revoke on any leak.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Scopes, consent phishing and refresh token rotation
md: Changing the password does not reliably remove an app's granted consent. RFC 9700 only says servers *may* revoke refresh tokens on a password change, and the consent record itself stays. Response to consent phishing means finding and revoking the app's consent and tokens, not just resetting credentials.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: GraphQL risks: introspection, batching and query depth
md: In GraphQL one request can mean one operation or thousands. Price requests by the work they ask for, check authorization where each field is resolved, and let the server, not the client, decide what is too expensive.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: How static analysis finds bugs: taint from source to sink
md: Source, propagation, sanitiser, sink. A finding is a path from a source to a sink with no sanitiser on it. False positives come from checks the tool cannot understand; false negatives come from sources, sinks or paths it does not model.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Prioritising with CVSS, EPSS and KEV, computed on real CVEs
md: KEV says "exploited now", EPSS says "likely soon", CVSS says "how bad if it happens", and your inventory says "where, how exposed, how important". Rank by evidence of exploitation and exposure first, severity second.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Restart part 1: analysis, then redo that repeats history
md: Redo is decided per page by LSN comparison alone, never by whether the transaction committed. Updates 80 and 100 belong to losers and are redone anyway. After redo the database is exactly as it was at the crash, and only then does undo begin.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Testing input types on your own data
md: Never assume the input type is right because results look plausible. Measure the grid of query and document settings on your own labeled queries, and keep tests that fail loudly when a call site or the index metadata drifts.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Inside Tokio's scheduler: local queues, stealing, LIFO slot
md: Tokio guarantees fairness only in a weak sense: if the number of tasks is bounded and no task blocks, every woken task is eventually scheduled. It does **not** promise round-robin order. Two ready tasks A and B may see A scheduled five times before B, even if A calls `yield_now`, a future that returns `Pending` once after arranging its own wakeup, so the scheduler may run something else first.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: From a waveform to 0.96 s log-mel patches
md: Clip length does not map to patches by simple division. YAMNet needs at least 0.975 s of audio (0.96 s plus the rest of the last 25 ms STFT window), pads anything shorter with silence, and rounds longer audio up to a whole hop. Our script gets 1 patch for 0.5 s, **2 patches for 1.0 s**, 10 for 5 s and 20 for 10 s.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Storing passwords wrong: plaintext, encryption, fast hashes
md: Hashing is not encryption. If a company can email you your old password, it is stored in plaintext or reversibly encrypted. A hash with no salt is only slightly better than plaintext against an attacker with a list of common passwords.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Kinds of MFA, and the maths inside a TOTP code
md: A TOTP code proves you hold the shared secret right now. It does not prove which website you are typing it into: anyone who sees the code within its 30-second window can use it once. Lesson 12 exploits exactly that gap.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Tracking sources and checking every citation
md: A citation that exists is not a citation that supports. Checking that every URL resolves catches invented sources but misses the more common failure: a real page cited for a claim it does not make.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: Below the API: Inferentia, Trainium, Neuron and SageMaker AI
md: Moving work onto Inferentia or Trainium is a **compiler** project as much as a hardware choice: your model must compile with Neuron, and custom ops may need NKI kernels. Budget engineering time for that, not just instance price.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Why weight bytes set the price of decoding
md: A 1.58-bit model is not a compressed full-precision model. It is a model whose weights were ternary during training, so nothing is lost when you ship the ternary weights.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Counters and history: how a predictor learns a pattern
md: A 2-bit counter can be fooled by alternation. For a branch that goes T, N, T, N, a counter starting at WN bounces between WN and WT and is wrong every single time (100 percent misses in our simulation). From the other start states it gets 50 percent. Agner Fog's manual describes this same worst case.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Compaction: merging sorted runs and organizing levels
md: Compaction converts a growing pile of overlapping files into a few large sorted runs. It is what keeps LSM reads and space bounded, and it is paid for with extra writes: every byte is rewritten each time it moves down a level.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: LRU-K: evict by the K-th most recent reference
md: LRU-K is not "keep the last K timestamps and you are done". Without a correlated reference period, a transaction that touches a page twice in a millisecond makes it look hot; without retained history, every page re-entering the pool starts at infinite distance and is evicted first.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Availability engineering: nines, redundancy and failure domains
md: Availability = uptime over total time. Hard dependencies multiply availabilities; independent redundant copies multiply failure rates; MTTR is a lever as strong as MTBF. Redundancy is only as good as its independence, so map failure domains, including software versions and admin identities.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Backups attackers cannot reach: immutability and isolated recovery
md: Assume production identity is lost. Give backups their own control plane, immutable and time-based retention, delayed and out-of-band-approved deletions, keys you cannot lose, alerts on every significant change, and restore into an isolated environment before anything returns to production.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Regulated resilience: DORA testing, TLPT and UK impact tolerances
md: DORA requires a BIA, backup and restore procedures with segregated restore systems, yearly continuity and switchover tests, a crisis function, and TLPT on production every three years for designated firms. The UK sets impact tolerances per important business service and requires proof, by severe but plausible scenario tests, that firms stay within them.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Generating with patches: the BLT decoding loop and its real cost
md: In BLT generation the latent model runs only when a patch closes, but the entropy model, encoder and decoder run on every byte in sequence. Fewer FLOPs per byte and lower latency are different goals; fixed patches, caches and speculative drafting are the levers for the second.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Data races: pthreads in C versus Send and Sync in Rust
md: Data race: unsynchronized conflicting accesses, undefined behavior, ruled out at compile time by the borrow rules plus Send and Sync. Race condition: a timing-dependent logic bug, still possible, still memory safe.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Why one load can cost 3 cycles or 240
md: Latency numbers are not constants of nature. Drepper's are for a Pentium M, CMU's for Haswell, and every CPU differs. Use them to reason about *ratios* (a DRAM access costs tens to hundreds of L1 hits), and measure your own machine before quoting absolute cycles.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Activation patching worked through: two directions and a shortcut
md: Denoising asks whether a component is enough to restore the behavior; noising asks whether the behavior needs it. AND-like circuits hide from denoising, OR-like backups hide from noising, and gradient shortcuts are trustworthy only for small patches.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Limitations, and tracing circuits yourself
md: An attribution graph explains one prompt in one replacement model. It is not proof of a general algorithm, it is silent about attention's choices, and any path through error nodes is unexplained. State those limits whenever you report a circuit.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Estimating propensities: swaps, EM, harvesting, dual learning
md: Pick the propensity source by how much user disruption you can afford: randomization or swaps are simplest and most trustworthy, EM and intervention harvesting use existing logs but rest on model assumptions, and DLA learns everything jointly. Every option inherits the click model's assumptions; if users behave like a cascade, a position-only propensity is misspecified.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Browser extensions: someone else's code in every page
md: Nothing on facebook.com was vulnerable in that case. An extension with access to a site is effectively a trusted script on that site. For a site owner this risk sits outside your perimeter; for an organisation that manages its employees' browsers, it is squarely inside it.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Where the evidence lives when there is no server to seize
md: Cloud incident response reconstructs what identities did through the provider's API, across four evidence layers: control plane, data plane, workload and identity provider. What you can prove is decided before the incident, by which logs were on and where they were kept.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Identity incidents: tokens, consent grants and mailbox rules
md: Misconception: "we reset the password, so the attacker is out". A reset leaves forwarding rules, registered MFA methods, OAuth consent grants and app passwords in place, and already issued access tokens keep working for up to about an hour in apps without CAE. Disable, revoke, then hunt for each kind of persistence.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: The same guardrails in Azure Policy and Google organization policy
md: Identity rules (RBAC, IAM) say who may act. Configuration guardrails (Azure Policy, Google organization policy, AWS SCPs used as preventive controls) say what no one may build, such as storage that accepts account keys or service accounts with downloadable keys. Set them high in the hierarchy, start in audit mode, then deny.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: The shared responsibility model, and when the provider gets it wrong
md: Common misconception: "we are on a big cloud, so the provider handles security." The provider secures its platform. Your identities, keys, data and configuration are yours, and even provider-side bugs usually ended with a customer to-do: regenerate keys after ChaosDB, update agents after OMIGOD.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Logging and detection: what key abuse looks like in CloudTrail
md: Log everything that changes configuration, keep it in a place attackers cannot reach, turn on data events for buckets that hold sensitive data, and alert on a short list of high-signal events: logging disabled, root use, new access keys and users, policy changes, and known credentials used from new places.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Choosing k: elbow, silhouette and their limits
md: Three things the silhouette cannot do. It is undefined for k = 1, so it can never tell you "this data has no clusters" (our k = 3 winner at 0.54 is not strong evidence of anything). It needs all pairwise distances, so it costs O(n squared) work. And it rewards compact well-separated blobs, so it is biased toward the kind of answer k-means produces, which makes it a poor referee between k-means and a density method.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Arrow in memory: buffers, validity bitmaps and offsets
md: A column in memory is a few flat buffers: values (or offsets plus data) and a validity bitmap. Flat, typed, contiguous buffers are what make tight loops and SIMD over columns possible.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Inlining: removing a call unlocks every other optimization
md: Misconception: the `inline` keyword forces inlining. It is a hint plus linkage rules: rules about how the function's definition is shared between files. At -O2 the compiler inlines functions you never marked, and may refuse ones you did. At -O0 GCC inlines nothing unless the function has `__attribute__((always_inline))`.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: PGO, -march=native and -ffast-math: speed with strings attached
md: -ffast-math assumes no NaNs or infinities (-ffinite-math-only), so code that relies on IEEE behavior of NaNs and infinities can give incorrect results. Clang has deprecated -Ofast because an optimization flag changing the observable behavior of correct code surprises people. Enable fast-math per file or per function when you have verified the numerics, not globally.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Safety: sandboxes, confirmations and prompt injection
md: Misconception: a system prompt saying "ignore instructions on web pages" solves injection. It helps, but the model reads that prompt and the attacker's text through the same channel. Defenses that do not depend on the model obeying (no secrets in the VM, network allowlists, harness-enforced confirmations) are what hold when the model is fooled.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Choosing and running loom and ThreadSanitizer in a real project
md: TSan must see **all** synchronization. Code not built with the flag (a prebuilt library, inline assembly) can cause false positives or missed races. That is why Rust's std should be rebuilt with the sanitizer via `-Zbuild-std`. The Rust unstable book also says Rust TSan does not support `std::sync::atomic::fence` or synchronization done in inline assembly, and rebuilding std does not change that.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Weaker but useful: sequential and causal consistency
md: Herlihy and Wing showed sequential consistency is **not local**: every object can be sequentially consistent while the system as a whole is not. Linearizability is local, which is one reason it composes better.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Must-haves and nice-to-haves need different machinery
md: Hard constraints decide **who is in**; soft constraints decide **the order**. Never let a preference buy its way past a requirement, and never let a preference silently remove someone.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: SAT solvers: DPLL, unit propagation and clause learning
md: CDCL = DPLL + conflict analysis that learns a clause + backjumping to the level where the learned clause becomes unit and forces (asserts) its last literal + watched literals for cheap propagation + activity-based decisions and restarts. Each conflict teaches the solver something it never has to rediscover.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Pinning by digest, signing images and verifying at admission
md: Pin by digest so you always run the same bytes; sign in CI and verify at admission so you only run bytes your pipeline produced.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Service account tokens and cloud identity for pods
md: A pod's identity is its service account token plus whatever cloud role it can reach. Mount tokens only where needed, give each app its own service account, and map cloud access per service account instead of per node.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Escapes in the runtime: runc CVE-2019-5736 and Leaky Vessels
md: Runtime escapes come from the runtime briefly holding host resources while entering a container. Patch the runtime everywhere, run only trusted images, and use user namespaces so that even a successful escape lands as an unprivileged user.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: The filters object and its four update operations
md: Deletes and resets are rare in training data and rare in casual testing, so they are the operations most likely to be broken in your system. Test them on purpose: write cases for *drop X*, *any X is fine*, *never mind the Y* and *start over*.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Storing state server-side and measuring it
md: Store the state server-side with a version and an event log; evaluate it with joint goal accuracy and per-operation recall, not just slot accuracy or end-to-end clicks.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Unfaithful without a hint: rationalization on natural prompts
md: Reversed question pairs detect unfaithfulness without planting anything: a consistent reasoner cannot answer Yes to both. This is behavioral evidence, necessary but not sufficient for faithful internal computation, and it shows frontier models rationalize rarely but measurably.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Streams, the default stream trap, and events
md: Three independent facts, often confused. A stream gives you **ordering** (and is always sequential inside itself). Separate streams give you **permission** to overlap. The hardware (`asyncEngineCount`, concurrent kernel support, free SMs) decides whether overlap actually **happens**. Two streams on a one-copy-engine GPU will still serialize their two transfers against each other.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Training a reranker: pointwise, pairwise, listwise and hard negatives
md: Hard negative mining has a trap: MS MARCO labels about one relevant passage per query, so many top-ranked unlabeled passages are actually relevant. Training to push them down teaches the model wrong lessons. mine_hard_negatives offers margins and a max_score cap partly to skip such false negatives.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: When hashes break: MD5, Flame and the SHA-1 collision
md: "It is only a checksum" is how MD5 and SHA-1 linger. Any place where an attacker can choose the input that gets hashed (certificates, signed documents, deduplication, commit ids, package lockfiles) needs collision resistance.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Padding oracles: when an error message decrypts your data
md: A padding oracle needs two things: decryption of unauthenticated ciphertext, and any observable difference (message, status code, timing, log line, connection reset) between padding failures and other failures. Remove the first and the second cannot matter: authenticate before you decrypt.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Never trust parameters: invalid curves, blank signatures, pinning
md: "The library checks that" is a claim to test, not assume. Java's verifier was a mainstream library. Run published test vectors such as Project Wycheproof against the exact library versions you ship.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: From MMA atoms to TiledMMA and TiledCopy
md: Atoms are hardware facts, TiledMMA and TiledCopy are spatial arrangements of atoms, and partition_A/B/C or partition_S/D (source and destination) turn a tile into per-thread fragments. Swapping the atom (FMA, mma.sync, wgmma) changes the instruction without rewriting the loops.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Worked example: what a CXL access costs
md: Do not assume every CXL device behaves like Pond's model. Sun et al. measured three real devices: one had load latency only 35% longer than a remote-socket DDR5 node, while the other two were about 2x and 3x longer. Their bandwidth efficiency also differed widely by controller. Emulating CXL with a remote NUMA socket, as early research did, can mislead in both directions.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Van Buren (2021): gates up or down, not good or bad motives
md: Van Buren is not a licence. Misusing data you may open can still be fraud, a privacy violation, a breach of contract, a firing offence or a state crime (lesson 4). And it says nothing about getting past a gate that is down: guessing a password or exploiting a bug to reach an area is still the off-limits kind.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Writing and selling tools: Marcus Hutchins and dual-use code
md: Writing security tools is legal almost everywhere. Laws target tools designed primarily for crime and people who supply them intending, or believing likely, criminal use. Context is evidence: who you sell to, how you advertise, what the features are for.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Evidence in court: authenticity, hearsay and chain of custody
md: Courts ask: is it what you say it is (authenticity), was it made routinely at the time (business records), and who could have changed it (chain of custody)? Automatic logs, hashes at collection and a tamper-evident custody record answer all three.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: The 3-step pipeline and what it did to The Pile
md: Using 280M-proxy weights for an 8B model is an empirical bet that good weights transfer across a 30x jump in scale. It paid off here, but the paper lists why weights transfer, and how far, as open questions, and its 1B proxy produced a worse 8B model than the 280M one (lesson 6). Weights also assume a token budget: lesson 5 shows what happens when you reuse them for a longer run.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Cleaning the crawl: heuristic rules, perplexity filters, exact dedup
md: Clean before you mix. Cheap rules remove describable junk, a perplexity filter keeps text resembling a reference (with its biases), and exact plus near deduplication removes copies. Each step shrinks domains, so redo the epoch math of lesson 5 and rerun the mixing step on the cleaned data.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Choosing a layout: hot/cold splits, ECS chunks and columnar data
md: List the hot loops, write down which fields each one touches and whether it streams or jumps, then pick the layout that packs those bytes together. Re-measure when the access pattern changes.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Tokens and masks: taking real values out of systems
md: Dynamic masking changes what is displayed, not what can be queried. Against anyone who can write their own WHERE clauses it is not a security boundary; use column permissions (lesson 8), tokens or encryption there.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a data security programme, and practice
md: Data security is a loop: find, label, keep less, protect, watch, destroy, with each finding feeding back into the inventory. Measure each stage, and judge controls by who can still cause the data to be read.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Honey records and honeywords: decoys inside your data
md: Our toy honeywords are small edits of the real password, which a smart attacker can often see through. The paper spends much of its length on generating decoys that are as likely as real user choices ("flatness"). Weak generation lets an attacker pick the real password far more often than 1 in $k$.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Why distributed bugs refuse to reproduce
md: DST makes a run a pure function of (code, seed). Faults can then be as aggressive and random as you like, because any failure they provoke can be replayed exactly by re-running one seed.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: CircleCI 2023: when the platform holding your secrets is breached
md: Encryption at rest did not save the secrets, because a running service must decrypt them to use them, and the attacker read the keys from a running process. The only secret a breached CI vendor cannot leak is one it never stored.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Sampling: predict every mask, keep the confident, remask the rest
md: A sampling step is: one forward pass over the whole sequence, a guess at every masked slot, then keep the k most confident guesses and remask the rest. The schedule fixes k per step; the confidence ranking decides the order.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Why prefill stalls decode on a shared GPU
md: Prefill is compute-bound and sets TTFT; decode is memory-bound and sets TPOT. Putting both in one batch makes each phase pay for the other.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: From sectors to partitions to image files
md: Do not stop at the partitions. NIST SP 800-86 counts *free space* (areas not allocated to any partition, including whole deleted volumes) as a place where data may remain. Our lab disk already has 2,047 sectors before the first partition that no file system owns.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Anti-forensics from the defender's side: what each trick leaves
md: The cleanup is evidence too. A 1102 event, a reset journal or deleted shadow copies at 14:35 tell you someone with administrator rights was covering tracks then, which often dates the intrusion better than anything they deleted.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Why DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop
md: DPO is not "RLHF without a reward". It fits the same Bradley-Terry reward model, just parameterized through the policy. It also inherits the KL objective's $\beta$. What it removes is the separate reward network and on-policy sampling during training.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Why a live data migration needs four careful phases
md: Until phase 4, at least one store is complete and current, and the other one is being kept in step with it. That is what makes every earlier step reversible. Plan each phase so it can be rolled out gradually (by percentage of objects or code paths) and rolled back with a flag.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Flipping writes, cutting over and deleting the old path
md: Move one thing at a time, keep one store complete until the very end, and measure agreement continuously. The deletion in phase 4 is the only step that should be hard to undo.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Affine quantization: storing reals as int8 plus a scale
md: Misconception: int8 means the model can only represent values between -128 and 127. The integers are codes; the scale maps them to any real range. What int8 limits is the number of distinct levels (256) inside that range, so the range you pick matters more than the bit width alone.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Ivanti Connect Secure, 2024: chained zero-days and a fooled checker
md: A clean integrity check is evidence, not proof. If an attacker reached root, the checker ran on a system the attacker controls. Trust measurements taken from outside the device, and rebuild when root was possible.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Overthinking: 901 tokens to say 2 + 3 = 5
md: Efficient reasoning asks a different question from test-time scaling. Not 'does more thinking help?' but 'how few thinking tokens reach the same accuracy on this particular problem?'

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Underthinking and early exit: stopping at the right moment
md: Long output does not tell you which failure you have. Overthinking re-solves an easy problem that was already right; underthinking abandons a promising approach on a hard one. The fixes differ: stop earlier in the first case, stay longer on each idea in the second.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Many spellings of one value: UTF-8 overlongs and base64 slack
md: Do not "fix" malformed input by cleaning it up and carrying on. Repairing an overlong sequence or dropping junk characters creates exactly the second spelling an attacker needs. Strict decoders that raise an error give every component the same answer: invalid.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Internationalised domain names, Punycode and what browsers show
md: Chromium's page is blunt that this is not a complete defence: it calls homographs "a limitation of how URLs are displayed in browsers in general" and lists other protections, such as Safe Browsing warnings and password managers that will not fill a password into a domain that is not exactly the right one. Treat the address bar as a hint, not a guarantee.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Where a sensor sits: kernel callbacks, minifilters and network filters
md: Misconception: "kernel mode makes a sensor untouchable." A kernel sensor can see everything, but so can any other code that reaches the kernel. An attacker who loads their own driver, or abuses a vulnerable signed one, is on equal footing with the sensor. That is exactly what the EDR-killer lesson covers.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Credential hardening: LAPS, LSA protection and Credential Guard
md: These controls each close one path: LAPS stops one local password from opening every machine; LSA protection stops ordinary processes reading LSASS; Credential Guard keeps the most reusable secrets out of LSASS's reach entirely; the ASR LSASS rule covers machines that can run neither. Check they are actually running, not just configured.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Scoring a disaggregation: MAE, NEP, NDE and F1
md: Metric details change numbers silently. The on/off threshold (10 W in NILMTK) sets F1; whether a paper reports NEP, NDE or energy accuracy changes which appliances look good; and per-appliance averages weight a lamp and a kettle equally while energy accuracy is dominated by the kettle. Always state the metric definition alongside a number.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: From pairwise links to entities: clustering
md: Blocking decides which pairs are compared, scoring decides which pairs are linked, and clustering decides which records share an ID. Tune the threshold on labeled data, because it trades false merges against missed merges.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Delegated vs application permissions, and who may consent
md: Misconception: an attacker needs an admin to consent before an app can steal mail. Delegated mail and file permissions are user-consentable by default, and the user's own mailbox is often the prize. Admin consent is needed for the tenant-wide versions, which is why attackers who compromise an admin go straight for application permissions.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Devices and the Primary Refresh Token: SSO bound to hardware
md: Misconception: a device-based Conditional Access rule means only company laptops get in. It means the token request came with a valid device identity. A device an attacker registers is a real device object, which is why device registration and join rights should be restricted and new registrations reviewed.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Taking over admins: help desks, MFA resets and rogue federation
md: Misconception: after a help-desk takeover, resetting the victim's password and MFA again evicts the attacker. If the attacker federated a domain or added an app credential, they can mint access without that account. Check federation settings, app credentials, role assignments and registered devices before calling it contained.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered, and reading until EAGAIN
md: Closing a descriptor removes it from the interest list only when **every** descriptor referring to the same open file is closed. If a `dup` or a `fork` left another copy open, events can keep arriving for a number you already closed. Call `EPOLL_CTL_DEL` before closing when duplicates may exist.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals by bootstrapping over queries
md: Resample queries, keep each query's pair of scores together, and report the interval along with the mean. A CI that crosses zero means your query set cannot tell the systems apart, whatever the point estimate says.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Why one leaked pointer defeats ASLR, and guessing at scale
md: ASLR is a secret, and like any secret it fails when leaked or when there are too few bits to stop guessing. Count the bits, avoid restart patterns that keep the secret constant, and treat information leaks as the first half of an exploit.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Fixing it: pad, align, or stop sharing writes
md: A fix needs both size and alignment: each hot item must start on a line boundary and be at least a line long. And pad only data that different threads write often; group everything else tightly.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: What the server sees: secure aggregation, DP, and Flower
md: The one thing to remember: federated learning is an optimization algorithm shaped by a systems constraint. Every piece (averaging instead of gradient sharing, a quorum instead of a barrier, masks instead of raw updates, noise instead of trust) exists because rounds are expensive, clients are unreliable, and the server is not allowed to look.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Putting it together: routing in DeepSeek-V3
md: Batch-level balance has two weak spots the report names: imbalance inside a single sequence or small batch, and **domain shift** at inference (a deployment flooded with one kind of input overloads that domain's experts). V3 answers the first with large training batches plus the tiny sequence-wise loss, and the second with redundant experts at serving time.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Revocation is hard: dbx space, SBAT and secure version numbers
md: Every anti-rollback step also breaks old *legitimate* media. KB5025885 warns that enabling the PCA 2011 revocation on a device with the April 2026 or later updates sets SVN 5.0 in firmware, which invalidates older external boot media. Rebuild recovery media before you raise the floor.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: Online softmax: exact attention one block at a time
md: Online softmax is exact. The running max is only for numerical safety (keeping $e^x$ from overflowing); any consistent reference point gives the same $O/l$. Every FlashAttention version computes the same math; they differ only in how the work is mapped onto the hardware.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: The training target: straight lines and their velocity
md: The training loss does not go to zero even for a perfect network. Different pairs pass through the same $(x_t, t)$ with different targets, and a regression can only output their average. That average is the field you want, as lesson 3 shows.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Refinement: proving a detailed design implements an abstract one
md: Implementation is implication: the detailed spec, seen through a refinement mapping, must allow only behaviors the abstract spec allows. Extra internal steps are fine because they map to stuttering steps.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: What 8 and 4 bits can hold: E4M3, E5M2 and E2M1
md: Exponent bits buy **range**, mantissa bits buy **precision**. E4M3 rounds with at most 6.25% relative error but spans only about 18 binades; E5M2 spans about 32 binades at 12.5%; E2M1 (FP4) spans 3.58 binades at up to 25%.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: NVFP4: 16-value blocks, E4M3 scales and a tensor scale
md: In NVFP4 the amax of every 16-value block is encoded at close to FP8 precision (the block scale is E4M3), which is at least 1/16 = 6.25% of all values. MXFP4 stores every value, the amax included, at FP4 precision behind a power-of-two scale.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Network and device signals: IPs, proxies and fingerprints
md: Never trust a device signal you did not verify. A header or a JavaScript value is a claim made by the client. Use it to raise suspicion when claims disagree or repeat across many accounts, not to grant trust on its own.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Promotion and referral abuse: multi-accounting and holds
md: Every promotion is a price per account. Tie it to a scarce identity, check the link between referrer and referee, and hold the payout until the qualifying payment can no longer be reversed.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: From risk score to decision: rules, models, step-up and review
md: Pick actions by expected cost: allow when $pL$ is small, block when $(1-p)G$ is small, and step up in between when the challenge catches more fraud than it costs in lost customers.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Why write() returning does not mean your data is safe
md: Calling fsync on a file does not necessarily make the file's **directory entry** durable. A newly created or renamed file also needs an fsync on a file descriptor for the directory, or after a crash the name may be missing.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: A real hunt with libFuzzer: harness, run log and the crash
md: A harness plus a sanitizer turns 'run the parser on generated bytes' into an automatic bug finder: coverage guidance reaches deep code, comparison tracing gets past magic values, and ASan converts silent corruption into a report with a saved reproducer.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Protocol and stateful fuzzing, and the Broadcom Wi-Fi case
md: Stateful targets need stateful fuzzing: keep a valid prefix, mutate later messages, use responses or coverage to recognise new states, and reset the target between sequences. Firmware that skips basic mitigations (no stack cookies) makes every such bug worse.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Filling the Wagner-Fischer table cell by cell
md: The table gives one number, but several different edit sequences can tie for the minimum. The traceback picks one of them. Do not read a single alignment as *the* explanation of how two strings differ.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: The Astrometry.net quad code, computed step by step
md: Invariant does not mean mirror-proof. Some cameras and optical paths flip the image. Astrometry.net's code-flip helper swaps each (x, y) pair, and the solver defaults to trying both parities (parity here means whether the image is mirrored or not). Groth's triangle method instead records whether vertices run clockwise and accepts either sense.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Radius search: cover with cells, then check exact distance
md: `WHERE ST_Distance(a, b) < 500` gives the right answer but cannot use the spatial index, so it scans every row. The PostGIS docs pair them deliberately: use `ST_DWithin` to limit the search with the index, then `ST_Distance` only for sorting the few survivors.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Why frameworks do not call cudaMalloc for every tensor
md: Misconception: "nvidia-smi shows 20 GB used, so my tensors use 20 GB." It shows reserved memory plus the CUDA context: the driver's per-process state on the GPU, such as loaded kernel code and the driver's own buffers, which uses device memory that PyTorch's counters never include. Compare `memory_allocated()` with `memory_reserved()` before hunting for a leak.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: From registers to HBM: the GPU memory map
md: **Local memory is not local to the chip.** The word refers to scope (one thread), not location. Spilled registers, large per-thread arrays and arrays indexed with values the compiler cannot resolve at compile time all go to local memory, which has the latency and bandwidth of global memory.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Case study: one matrix transpose, three kernels
md: The NVIDIA post's conclusion: coalescing global memory accesses is by far the most critical step. Use shared memory to turn strided global access into coalesced access, then check the shared access for bank conflicts.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: How profiling perturbs what it measures
md: Decide which question you are asking before you choose the flags. Isolated-kernel analysis wants the defaults: locked clocks, flushed caches, serialized launches. System-representative behavior wants `--replay-mode application --clock-control none --cache-control none`. Mixing the two across runs produces numbers that disagree for reasons that have nothing to do with your code.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: From chunks to an entity graph with LLM extraction
md: The graph is an LLM's *abstractive summary* of the corpus (written in the model's own words, not copied sentences), not a parse of it. Every node and edge carries an LLM-written description, and those descriptions, not the raw text, are what later stages summarize.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: RLVR: replacing the reward model with a program
md: Verifiable does not mean perfect. A verifier can reject correct answers (12.0 versus 12) or accept wrong ones (a unit-test suite that misses edge cases). Real pipelines normalize answers; for example, Tulu 3's 'flex' MATH evaluation tries three different ways to extract the final answer, because models often ignore the requested format. The quality of the checker caps the quality of the signal.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: What a GTFS Schedule zip contains and how its tables join
md: A stop can appear twice in one trip, for example on a loop route where the bus starts and ends at the same stop. That is why `stop_sequence`, not `stop_id`, identifies a row of a trip. Code that keys stop times by `stop_id` alone silently overwrites one visit with the other.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Phone phreaking: when the voice line was also the control line
md: Filtering out the 2600 Hz tone would have been a weak fix: phreaks used many other tones, and a filter on a shared channel is always a race. Removing the attacker's access to the control channel ended the whole class of trick.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Conficker: the botnet that made the industry organise
md: Conficker showed both sides of collective defence: an industry coalition could deny a botnet its control channel at internet scale, but cleaning millions of unmanaged PCs was beyond it. Patching (MS08-067 was a month old) and removing risky defaults (AutoRun) would have prevented most infections.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: SolarWinds and Log4Shell: what you install and what you import
md: SolarWinds attacked what you install (a trusted vendor's build), Log4Shell lived in what you import (a free library inside other products). The responses were inventory (SBOMs), verifiable builds, least privilege for powerful tools like network monitors, and review boards that turn incidents into public lessons.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: What a side channel is: secrets leaking through how code runs
md: A side-channel attack does not break the mathematics. It breaks the assumption that an implementation reveals only its outputs. Every defence in this course makes some byproduct independent of the secret, hides the secret from the computation that leaks, or keeps the observer away.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: One request, two readers: why proxies and caches disagree
md: Testing a site's proxies or cache for these bugs can harm *other* users, because the leftover bytes or poisoned entries land on real people. Test only systems you own or have written permission to test, and prefer your own lab: the toys in this course run entirely in one Python process.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: How HTTP caches decide: keys, freshness and Vary
md: A cache key is a promise: "any two requests with this key deserve the same response". Every attack in the next lessons breaks that promise, either because the response depended on something outside the key, or because two different resources ended up under one key.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: hugetlbfs: a reserved pool you map on purpose
md: A pool is memory you have given away. Those 3170 pages hold 6.2 GiB out of the page cache (the kernel's in-memory cache of file data) and away from every other process whether or not PostgreSQL is running. Over-sizing `nr_hugepages` is a common way to cause out-of-memory kills on a box that looks half empty.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Counting cache bytes: growing KV cache plus a fixed state
md: Hybrids do not help much at short context. At 1,024 tokens the cache formula gives only about 1.9x less memory for Nemotron-H-8B, and both the Jamba and NVIDIA papers report similar speed to Transformers at small context lengths. The gains grow with context and batch size.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Why a raw query is a poor probe for an unsupervised encoder
md: Short queries and long documents look different. A label-free encoder knows what *documents* resemble each other, but nobody taught it what *answers a question*. HyDE's trick is to stop comparing a question with answers at all.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Zones and conduits: the ISA/IEC 62443 way to segment
md: Zones are not VLANs. A VLAN (virtual LAN) is one way to separate traffic, but NIST lists VLANs as logical separation 'when physical separation may not be feasible'. A zone boundary needs an enforcement point, and a misconfigured switch trunk can quietly merge two zones.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Segmentation, DMZs, one-way gateways and allowlisting
md: A firewall rule that says 'allow 10.0.0.0/8 to OT, any port, temporary' is the most common way segmentation fails. Review the rule table regularly, expire temporary rules automatically, and alert on hits to rule 11: traffic nobody planned is either a misconfiguration or an intruder.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Inside a SAML response: Issuer, Subject, Conditions and statements
md: Attributes are authorization input. An SP that maps `groups=admins` in the assertion to admin rights hands role decisions to whoever controls assertion content: the IdP's administrators, anyone who compromises them, and anyone who can get an unsigned assertion past the SP.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Conditional access: deciding at sign-in, and what happens after
md: Conditional access decides at the moment of issuance. Everything after that moment is protected by token lifetime, session binding and signals, so a policy is only as strong as the session it produces.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Leavers: deprovisioning, SCIM and the Cash App download
md: Disabling the IdP account is not deprovisioning. It blocks the next single sign-on. Sessions already open, tokens already issued, local accounts and shared passwords all survive it.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Measuring identity hygiene, detecting abuse, and running the programme
md: Measure the tail, not just the median: one leaver with 400 hours of access matters more than a good average. Pair hygiene metrics (orphans, dormant, standing privilege, owners) with detections for terminated logins, out-of-process grants, vault and break-glass use.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Events, alerts and incidents: when does it become an incident?
md: An incident starts when the attacker acts, not when you declare it. The HSE intrusion began on 18 March 2021 and was declared on 14 May. The gap (dwell time) is what your logs, memory and timeline work must reach back across.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Acquisition: memory, disk images, cloud snapshots and logs
md: Encryption changes the plan. If a disk uses BitLocker or another full-disk encryption, an image taken after power-off is unreadable without the recovery key. Capture what you need from the running system, or make sure the key is in your hands before you shut it down.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Blameless postmortems, lessons learned and tabletop exercises
md: Blameless does not mean nobody is accountable. It means the review asks why the system let a reasonable person make that choice, and fixes the system: alert routing, ownership, tooling, training.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Why epoll plus read still costs a syscall per I/O
md: epoll is a **readiness** API: it tells you when an operation *could* succeed, then you do it. io_uring is a **completion** API: you describe the operation (read these bytes into this buffer), and the kernel tells you when it is *done* and what it returned.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Threat modelling a device: who can reach it, and how
md: A common mistake is to skip the physical position because "attackers would need the device". Attackers can buy the device. The right question is what one opened unit gives them: its owner's data (acceptable for many products) or a key to all units (never acceptable).

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Medical devices: FDA section 524B, pacemakers and insulin pumps
md: A medical maker cannot ship fixes as casually as a phone maker: each change may need risk review, and an implant update happens in a clinic. That is why FDA expects the update path and the postmarket plan to be designed before approval, not invented after a disclosure.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Fixing ReDoS: rewrite, bound, change engines, cap the input
md: Both V8 modes are experimental, and the blog says the fallback skips patterns with backreferences, lookarounds, large bounded repeats, or the `u` and `i` flags. Treat the flag as a safety net that you test with your own patterns, not as the fix. Rewriting and bounding input are the fixes.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: One skeleton, three allocators: size classes and caches
md: Every production allocator is the same four layers: size classes, a lock-free local cache, a shared per-size-class middle, and a page-level back-end that talks to the OS. The interesting differences are *who owns the local cache* (thread, CPU, or page), *how objects freed by another thread get home*, and *when idle pages go back to the OS*.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Elle: catching isolation anomalies in transactions
md: Elle never solves for a transaction order. It designs the workload so reads expose the version order, then turns the history into a dependency graph and looks for cycles. A cycle is a concrete, explainable counterexample, and its edge types name the anomaly.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The per-packet budget: why the kernel path runs out of cycles
md: Kernel bypass means the **device driver lives in your process**. Data moves between device and application memory by DMA, the application learns about it by polling memory, and nothing on the per-packet or per-I/O path enters the kernel.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: Driver signing: from cross-signing to Microsoft's portal
md: Misconception: "since 2016 only Microsoft-signed drivers load." Only *new* drivers had to go through Microsoft. Drivers already signed under the cross-signing program, with leaf certificates from before 29 July 2015, kept loading on most systems for a decade. Many drivers later abused in BYOVD attacks date from that era.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: Kernel Data Protection and PatchGuard: guarding data, catching patches
md: Misconception: "PatchGuard makes kernel tampering impossible." Microsoft's own description is narrower: it detects certain modifications and shuts the system down, and it does not prevent all malware. In the BlackByte case, Sophos reported that security callbacks were removed regardless. Treat KPP as a tripwire, not a wall.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Limits of fusion and how compilers decide
md: A fusion is worth it when it removes HBM round trips or launches without blowing the on-chip budget or recomputing expensive work. Compilers estimate bytes saved, check legality, and fuse greedily; in training they also choose between saving and recomputing activations.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Matching what the teacher computes inside: hints, attention, states
md: Hints match a teacher layer through a learned regressor; attention transfer sums channels away so widths need not match; TinyBERT matches attention matrices and hidden states layer by layer through a mapping g(m); DistilBERT aligns last-layer directions with a cosine loss.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sharing keys and values across heads: MQA and GQA
md: GQA and MQA are architecture choices. They need training (or uptraining) and cannot be switched on at serving time, but they stack with every serving-time trick in the rest of this course.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Compressing long prompts (SnapKV, PyramidKV) and choosing a recipe
md: Choose by failure mode: FP8 for a near-free 2x; per-channel-key, per-token-value low-bit (KIVI, KVQuant) for 4x to 5x if kernels support it; eviction (StreamingLLM, H2O, SnapKV, PyramidKV) when context length is the problem and occasional lost tokens are acceptable.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Eviction and placement: what stays, what sinks, what is dropped
md: Do not evict a prefix's parent before its children. Because keys are chained, removing an early block makes every later block of that prefix unreachable, yet those stranded blocks still occupy space. SGLang's radix tree evicts leaves first for this reason, and Mooncake Store can evict a group of related objects (such as the separate K and V tensors of one entry) all or none.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Why one vector per document leaves accuracy behind
md: ColBERT is not a cross-encoder with a trick. Query tokens never attend to document tokens inside the transformer. All query-document interaction happens in MaxSim, which has no trainable parameters. That is exactly why document vectors can be stored in advance.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Why reasoning in word tokens is a bottleneck
md: Coconut's one change: in latent mode, the next input embedding is the previous position's last hidden state instead of the embedding of a sampled token.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Why superposition works: continuous thoughts and graph reachability
md: A continuous thought can hold a whole reachable set at once, so one step expands every branch in parallel. D thoughts suffice for a graph of diameter D, while a discrete chain must name one node per step.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Error windows, exponential search and monotonic models
md: Always handle the case where the search lands on the edge of the window. With stored min/max bounds, a hit on the boundary is the signal that a non-monotonic model may have pushed the true answer outside.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: Why ranking needs its own loss function
md: Ranking metrics depend on the scores only through the **sort**. Learning to rank works around that either by optimizing a smooth stand-in loss (RankNet, ListNet) or, in LambdaRank and LambdaMART, by writing down the gradient we want directly. The coming lessons build each of these.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The state is a key-value memory, and it fills up
md: The state is a key-value memory with room for about $d_k$ clean associations per head. Linear attention writes to it with a purely additive rule, so it can neither correct an old association nor make room for new ones.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Where things live: the Linux filesystem from a defender's view
md: Learn the map once: configuration in `/etc`, user secrets in `/home` and `/root`, shared scratch in `/tmp`, history in `/var/log`, the live view in `/proc`. Almost every later lesson points at one of these places.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: SSH: keys versus passwords, authorized_keys and hardening
md: Turning off password login does not help if an attacker can write to `authorized_keys`, and a private key copied from a laptop works from anywhere. Protect private keys with a passphrase, remove keys of people who leave, and review every `authorized_keys` file on your servers, including root's (`/root/.ssh/authorized_keys`).

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: CIS Benchmarks: what one recommendation contains
md: Applying Level 2, or even all of Level 1, to production without testing is how hardening projects cause outages. CIS itself recommends trying the guidance in a test environment first. A benchmark is a starting point that you tailor (next lessons), not a script to run blind.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Writing audit rules that answer real questions
md: `-w` watches are the older syntax; audit.rules(7) calls them deprecated and slower, recommending `-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -F path=... -F perm=wa` instead. Many published baselines still use `-w`, and both work. And remember the limit: audit sees system calls. Lesson 13 shows activity that never makes one.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Linux EDR and fleet telemetry: what sensors see and miss
md: Do not set kernel.io_uring_disabled fleet-wide without checking workloads: io_uring exists for performance, and some of your workloads may use it. This is a tailoring decision per host class (lesson 4).

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Immutable OS images: rebuild instead of repair
md: Immutable images make the OS read-only and replace it whole: drift and most persistence disappear, patching becomes shipping a tested image, and runtime telemetry focuses on the few writable areas. The price is new ways to debug and to run agents.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: BLEU, ROUGE and BERTScore, and where they fail
md: Overlap metrics measure closeness to a reference, not correctness. A fluent answer with one wrong fact can outscore a correct paraphrase. They also penalize outputs that are better than, but different from, the reference, which is common once a strong LLM writes the outputs.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Inside an inference server: one engine step at a time
md: The scheduler decides **what** runs each step, the KV cache manager decides whether it **fits**, and the executor just runs a forward pass over token ids and block tables. Almost every serving optimization in this course is a change to the first two.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: When the pool runs dry: admission control and preemption
md: Admission control is a bet about future output lengths. Reserve the worst case and you never preempt but waste memory; allocate on demand and you fit far more requests but need a preemption policy (latest arrival first, all of its blocks) and a recovery method (swap or recompute).

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Why hard constraints need filters, not similarity
md: The LLM never touches the documents. It only translates the query into a filter object. Exact enforcement is done by the search engine, which is cheap, deterministic and testable.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Calls and tokens per query for each method
md: Calls set the latency floor and the per-call overhead; tokens set the bill. Listwise minimizes calls, not tokens. PRP buys robustness to prompt order with 20 to 100 times more prompts than pointwise (220 to 1,100 times more than listwise) at k = 100.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pointwise: yes/no relevance and query likelihood
md: Both pointwise methods need token log-probabilities. Many chat APIs only return generated text, which is why the RankGPT authors could not run them on GPT-4. And because each passage is scored alone, the score must be comparable across passages (calibrated), which the PRP paper argues LLMs are not trained to provide.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: SIFT: keypoints across scale and a 128-number descriptor
md: A SIFT keypoint carries position, scale and orientation. The descriptor is computed in that local frame, which is why it survives zoom and rotation, and its 128 entries are L2-normalized and clipped for lighting robustness.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The Treiber stack: one CAS on the top pointer
md: Pop reads `old->next` after loading `old` but before its CAS. If another thread pops `old` and frees it in that gap, the read touches freed memory. Worse, if the node is reused before the CAS, the CAS can still succeed with a stale `next`. That is the ABA problem, and it is the subject of the next lesson.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Drain: a fixed-depth parse tree and a similarity threshold
md: The one thing to remember: Drain bounds the work per line to a fixed tree walk plus a comparison against the few groups in one leaf, which makes its cost $O(n)$ in the number of lines. It buys that speed with two assumptions, that same-template lines share a token count and that early tokens are constants.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Normalisation: one event, one shape (ECS and OCSF)
md: A Windows 4625 converted to ECS and an sshd failure converted to ECS look identical to a rule, which is the point, but also a risk: a mapping mistake (say, putting the target host into source.ip) now breaks every rule at once. Test mappings with sample events from each source, exactly like rules (lesson 11).

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Baselines, anomalies and UEBA: how Storm-0558 was caught
md: State's advantage was not a product; it was three years of studying normal mailbox access, which let a modest-looking event stand out. The CSRB notes that buying the logs alone would not have been enough: few organisations analysed that voluminous log in detail.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Attention memory and Ring Attention
md: Ring Attention is not an approximation like sparse attention (each query sees only a chosen subset of keys) or sliding-window attention (each query sees only a fixed window of recent tokens). Each query still attends to every key; only the *order* and *location* of the work change. It also does not reduce FLOPs: total compute is the same quadratic amount, just spread over more chips.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: What a loop can compute: algorithms, latent thoughts, fixed points
md: A loop is an algorithm's inner step. With enough iterations, a fixed-size block can resolve chains of references, simulate a small computer, or stand in for chain-of-thought steps, without adding parameters. How well *training* finds such a step is a separate, empirical question.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Learned depth per token: Mixture-of-Recursions, Ouro, HRM and TRM
md: Do not compare TRM's ARC numbers with LLM results as if they were the same kind of system. TRM is trained per task family on about 1000 augmented examples with a fixed answer grid; an LLM is a general text model. An independent ARC Prize analysis cited by the TRM paper found deep supervision drove most of HRM's gain (19% to 39%), while the two-level recursion added little (35.7% to 39.0%).

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: The wider PEFT family, and when LoRA falls short
md: Hu et al.'s footnote already warned that a small rank should not be expected to work for every task: if the target were a different language than pretraining, full fine-tuning (like LoRA with r equal to the model width) could win. Low intrinsic rank was measured on tasks that are close to what the model already knows.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Unlearning by replacement: Who's Harry Potter and RMU
md: Near-chance accuracy on a multiple-choice proxy shows the model no longer *answers* those questions. It does not show the knowledge is gone from the weights. The WMDP authors say so themselves: because RMU edits only three layers it "perhaps obfuscates knowledge more than unlearns it", and in their appendix fine-tuning on the forget corpus recovered the performance.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: How a Mac defends itself: the layers from boot to app
md: "Macs don't get viruses" is a myth defenders still meet. Information stealers such as Atomic Stealer (lesson 16) have been sold to criminals as a monthly service since 2023, and Microsoft documented new campaigns delivering them to Macs in 2026. The built-in controls are strong, but they mostly decide what may *launch*; social engineering goes around them.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Unified logging: reading what the Mac recorded
md: Do not expect an attacker's password prompt, curl URL or file path to show up in plain text in the unified log. Default privacy redaction hides many dynamic strings. Plan on Endpoint Security or EDR telemetry for process command lines, and use the unified log for subsystem state changes.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: What malware is, and the families analysts name
md: NIST notes that most samples blend several categories, so the classic labels are 'considerably less useful than they used to be' for incident handling. Use the labels to communicate quickly; spend your time on behaviour and detection.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Behaviours as indicators: persistence, credentials, ransomware
md: Every behaviour rule has false positives: per-user installers for chat and sync clients legitimately write Run keys from AppData. Sigma's falsepositives field is not decoration; tune with an allowlist of known-good signed programs and review what fires.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Why vector size is a cost knob, and why chopping a vector fails
